faqs.q: What drives the cost of a wildlife job in a low, marsh-edge Grove home?
faqs.a: Access and foundation condition. Pier foundations and tight, damp crawlspaces take longer to inspect and seal than a standard basement home, and skirting or vent replacement is often part of the real fix rather than an extra. We crawl what can be crawled, photograph the openings we find under there, and quote the removal plus the foundation repairs together, so you are not paying twice for two halves of one job.

faqs.q: Bats come out of my Grove attic every evening at dusk — what kind are they, and what happens next?
faqs.a: On the James River edge the usual attic tenants are big brown bats and evening bats, both drawn by the insect life over the marsh creeks. Whatever the species, Virginia bat work is exclusion only: one-way exits at the active gaps, every other opening sealed, and the colony leaves on its own — relocation of bats is unlawful in Virginia. Exclusions are scheduled outside the maternity season under DWR permit conditions, and a bat found to be a listed species turns the job into a referral to the Department of Wildlife Resources instead.

Grove.wildlife_intro:
Grove has lived beside the James River longer than Williamsburg has been a tourist town, and its wildlife is tidal-country wildlife. Marsh creeks behind the houses feed raccoons year-round, evening bats and big brown bats work the river edge at dusk and roost in the low, warm attics of Grove's older cottages, and black rat snakes follow rodents into pier foundations and crawlspaces all along the Route 60 corridor. On the ground, opossums and skunks den under the skirting and stoops of the community's many low-set homes.

Low ground is the theme of every Grove job. A crawlspace that stays damp rots the very vents and skirting meant to keep animals out, so we pair every removal with foundation work that can survive the marsh edge: proper vent covers, repaired skirting, and caps and screens fitted where the roof meets the trees. Grove homeowners hear the same advice from us every visit — fix the low openings first, because the river will keep sending tenants to test them.

faqs.q: How do you quote work on a Lanexa river house that is only used on weekends?
faqs.a: Part-time occupancy usually means the problem has had time to grow — a bat colony in its second summer or a raccoon family plus a season of attic damage — so the inspection, not the calendar, sets the price. We inspect the house and the outbuildings together, quote the removal, cleanup, and sealing as one written scope, and flag the prevention items that matter most for a house that sits empty, so you can judge the priorities yourself.

faqs.q: Canada geese have taken over my Lanexa dock lawn — can you get rid of them?
faqs.a: Not by removal — Canada geese are federally protected, and no Virginia nuisance permit covers taking them. What does work on reservoir and river lawns is making the grass less inviting: a planted buffer of taller vegetation at the water's edge, which geese dislike crossing, consistent hazing when they first arrive in spring, and never feeding them. Nest and egg work exists only inside a federal depredation framework that requires registering with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service first — we can explain how that registration works, but we will not sell you a goose removal that does not legally exist.

Lanexa.wildlife_intro:
Between the Chickahominy River and Diascund Reservoir, Lanexa is more forest and water than neighborhood — and a good share of its houses sit empty between weekends. Empty houses are an open invitation: raccoons den undisturbed in cottage chimneys, big brown bat colonies grow in quiet reservoir-side attics, and gray squirrels chew into eaves that nobody hears for a month. At the water's edge, beavers work the reservoir coves and riverbanks, and Canada geese claim the mowed lawns that run down to docks.

Our Lanexa work leans toward prevention for part-time homes. A spring opening inspection — chimney, attic, crawlspace, boat shed, in that order — catches most problems while they are still small, and the sealing we do is chosen to hold through months with nobody home. For the geese on the lawn, expect honest deterrence talk rather than removal talk: geese are federally protected, and the lasting fixes are habitat and hazing, not a service call that pretends otherwise.
